title: Air Pollution: 30,000 Deaths a Year and What Government Can Do
label: 14 September 2026 · Air pollution and public health
summary: The Environmental Audit Committee questioned the Public Health Minister, England's Chief Medical Officer and a senior health official about the damage caused by air pollution and whether the Government is doing enough to prevent it. The witnesses estimated that air pollution contributes to around 30,000 deaths annually, alongside serious illness throughout people's lives. Pollution has fallen substantially, but poorer communities remain especially vulnerable, and there is no level of pollution known to be completely safe. The discussion covered cleaner transport, farming, heating, housing decisions, medical advice and public awareness. Professor Whitty argued that further reductions are achievable and would bring major health benefits. Committee members pressed the Government to strengthen pollution limits, protect vulnerable communities and communicate risks more openly. The Minister acknowledged the need for further action but made no commitment to tougher legal limits or a national awareness campaign.

glossary.definition: The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which leads the Government's work on air pollution limits and environmental policy.
The World Health Organization, a United Nations agency that publishes health advice, including recommended limits for air pollution.
The National Health Service, which provides publicly funded healthcare in the UK.
A gas released by farming activities, particularly manure and fertilisers, that can react with other substances in the air to form harmful particles.
Extremely small airborne particles, no more than 2.5 micrometres wide, that can travel deep into the lungs and affect the heart and other organs.
A harmful gas produced by burning fuel, particularly in vehicle engines, which can irritate the lungs and worsen breathing problems.
A professional organisation representing doctors that publishes medical research, guidance and reports on public health.
A research project investigating how London's air pollution and changes in traffic emissions affect children's lung health.
London's Ultra Low Emission Zone, where vehicles that fail to meet specified emissions standards must pay a daily charge.
An infectious bacterial disease that usually affects the lungs and can cause serious illness.
A scale showing how polluted the air is on a particular day, helping people judge potential health risks.
A group brought together by DEFRA, involving researchers, health professionals and charities, to improve public information about air pollution.
The public health agency responsible for protecting people in England from infectious diseases and other health threats.
The European Union, a group of European countries that share rules and policies in several areas, including environmental standards.
A proposed UK law, also called Ella's Law, seeking to establish a legal right to clean air and stronger duties to control pollution.

chapters.title: The health damage and its causes
chapters.takeaway: Air pollution contributes to tens of thousands of deaths and many serious illnesses, but cleaner technology and changes to everyday activities could reduce the damage substantially.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're examining how the Government deals with air pollution. I'm disappointed that the department responsible for housing and local government has declined to send anyone. Housing decisions, construction and local monitoring all matter here. Minister, how easy is it to get other government departments to take the health consequences seriously?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: I've only been in this role for a few weeks, but there are established relationships between departments. Air pollution can't be left to the Health Department or DEFRA, which leads on environmental policy. Every department has a part to play. Our job is to provide the medical evidence so that health is considered when other departments make decisions.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: The evidence links air pollution to between 26,000 and 38,000 deaths a year, alongside long-term illness and substantial costs to the NHS. DEFRA is reviewing the national air quality strategy, which gives us an opportunity to improve how departments work together.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Professor Whitty, what exactly does air pollution do to people's health?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: It affects people throughout their lives. It increases the risk of premature birth, severe childhood asthma and poor lung development. In adults, it's a major cause of heart disease and stroke, which many people don't realise. It also contributes to long-term lung disease and some cancers, particularly lung cancer. There's growing evidence connecting it with dementia.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: The Royal College of Physicians gives a central estimate of around 30,000 deaths annually. That's an estimate, not an exact count. But there's also an enormous opportunity to prevent illness. Reducing pollution, alongside reducing smoking, could give today's children much healthier lungs than previous generations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Where is the pollution coming from?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Transport is a major source, although vehicle emissions have fallen significantly. Electric vehicles should reduce them further. Construction also matters. Farming releases ammonia, which contributes to harmful particles in the air, and unlike most pollutants, ammonia emissions haven't fallen much over time. Heating buildings is another important source, particularly during winter.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Which types of heating are the most polluting?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Heating that burns fuel produces pollution. Electric heating doesn't release it inside the home. Oil heating produces some, wood-burning stoves generally produce more, and older stoves and open fires are especially polluting. There's a clear difference between these options.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What practical changes would make the biggest difference?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: International action is crucial because pollution crosses borders. Some of the harmful particles in our air come from continental Europe, and some of ours travel there. Shared European vehicle standards have helped reduce pollution without putting manufacturers in one country at a disadvantage.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: There are simpler changes too. I can't understand why we still let diesel trains sit with their engines running in stations just to keep the lights on, when an electricity supply is metres away. That creates unnecessary pollution around passengers and staff. We could stop that relatively quickly.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Agriculture is another opportunity. Some countries have reduced ammonia emissions by changing farming practices. Those changes can ultimately save farmers money because they need less fertiliser. We should learn how they've achieved that.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The UK's legal pollution limits are less demanding than the WHO's health recommendations. Even if we meet our targets, people could still suffer serious health effects. Should we aim higher?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Yes. We should reduce pollution as far as we reasonably can while keeping the economy and society functioning. We can make substantial progress without damaging the economy. Targets are useful, but reaching them shouldn't mean stopping. Every further reduction can prevent illness, and people generally support cleaner air.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: If the current legal limits still allow pollution that causes premature deaths and illness, why are we keeping them?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: We recognise that there's no level of air pollution known to be completely harmless. We want levels to fall further. DEFRA sets the legal targets, and its forthcoming review will provide an opportunity to consider the latest scientific and medical evidence.

chapters.title: Why poorer communities face greater risks
chapters.takeaway: People in disadvantaged areas often face both higher pollution and poorer underlying health, but measuring whether policies reduce that inequality remains difficult.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: Air pollution particularly affects children, poorer communities, ethnic minority groups and people who already have health conditions. What are we doing to reduce those inequalities, and how will we know whether it's working?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Our ten-year health plan aims to halve the difference between rich and poor in the number of years people can expect to live in good health. Local public health teams can now use information showing pollution levels alongside details about residents' ages and economic circumstances. That helps councils identify areas where children, older people or other vulnerable groups need particular attention.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: The CHILL study, involving children in London and Luton, is especially interesting. It examined changes in air pollution, including London's ULEZ policy, and showed the potential for children's lungs to recover and grow when the air gets cleaner. Local mayors can consider policies suited to their communities. But we still need better ways to measure whether our wider health policies are succeeding.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: Are you saying local authorities should be responsible for monitoring these problems?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: They have a major role, particularly in helping disadvantaged neighbourhoods. But national government and international action remain important too. Councils and elected mayors can make decisions that reflect their communities' particular circumstances.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: My concern isn't giving local authorities responsibility. It's whether they're getting enough money to carry it out.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: I can't speak for the department responsible for local government, but councils have received additional funding over the past two years. Local NHS services also work with councils to assess community health needs. Central government still has responsibilities here.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: We may need to ask the housing and local government department directly about the funding. Professor Whitty, how should we measure progress?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: People in deprived areas often suffer twice. On average, they start with poorer health and are then exposed to worse pollution. That makes the effects particularly serious. But because pollution spreads widely, reducing it for everyone will usually bring the greatest overall benefit, including to poorer communities.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: We can measure pollutants and identify where vulnerable people live. But the resulting estimate of health damage is calculated rather than directly observed. It's much easier to judge a policy when we measure people's health before and after a specific change. That's what makes studies such as CHILL valuable. We should do more of that, rather than simply assume our policies are working.

chapters.title: Medical advice, monitoring and indoor air
chapters.takeaway: Doctors need better ways to advise patients, pollution monitoring should focus more closely on vulnerable groups, and indoor air quality deserves much greater attention.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: I recently met a nurse who'd developed tuberculosis. Her specialist hadn't discussed how air pollution might affect her illness. Are doctors being given enough guidance to explain these risks, particularly to patients with breathing problems, heart conditions or pregnancy-related vulnerabilities?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Air pollution is clearly linked to tuberculosis and other respiratory infections. Most doctors understand that pollution is harmful. The harder question is what they can tell an individual patient to do about it. Someone can stop smoking, but they can't simply stop breathing polluted air. People at high risk can use pollution forecasts to adjust their activities on particularly bad days, but society-wide reductions are far more effective.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: Are we monitoring pollution and the illnesses it causes closely enough?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Our monitoring isn't bad, but it's far from ideal. I'd like a denser network of pollution monitors, especially in towns and cities where most of the risks occur. We should pay particular attention to schools, care homes and hospitals. That would help us understand what vulnerable people are breathing and whether local improvements are working.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about people living right beside busy roads? Housing authorities might place a family with a child who has asthma in a particularly polluted home. Is government doing enough to identify and protect people facing those higher risks?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: If you look at pollution maps of major cities, the busiest roads stand out clearly because of higher nitrogen dioxide and particle pollution. Airports can create similar problems. Ideally, we wouldn't place the most vulnerable people in those locations. But reducing pollution across the whole city remains the single most important intervention.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Beyond reducing pollution generally, are departments using the medical evidence properly when they make decisions about housing, healthcare and people's everyday lives?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: On outdoor pollution, I think government departments genuinely work together. DEFRA and the Department for Transport both take this seriously. As a doctor, I'd always like faster progress, but I don't think poor coordination is the main obstacle in those departments.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Indoor pollution is different. Our understanding is less developed, and government coordination is weaker. As outdoor air has improved, indoor pollution has become relatively more important. I'd prioritise public buildings such as hospitals, libraries, supermarkets and places of worship. People often have no choice about entering them, and they can't easily tell whether the air is polluted.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Private homes are more complicated. We should provide people with information, but there's a difference between advising them and telling them how to live. We also have much less scientific evidence about indoor pollution than outdoor pollution.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: What are we doing to make sure doctors can advise patients properly? How close are we to making that normal practice throughout the NHS?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: All doctors should learn about air pollution at medical school, with more specialised training for doctors treating children, pregnant women and people with lung or heart problems. Professional medical organisations have made progress, but there's more to do. If I had to invent a rough figure, I'd say we're perhaps halfway there. That's not a measured percentage.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Doctors aren't the only people who can help. Health visitors and other healthcare professionals who work with families can explain risks and help parents identify practical ways to protect their children.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: Are local NHS organisations actually required to identify and act on air pollution risks, or can they choose whether to do so?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Local NHS organisations and councils assess the health needs of their communities. They need to work together, identify local risks and consider how to communicate with residents. That involves the organisations funding and providing healthcare, public health teams and local authorities.

chapters.title: Should the public be warned more clearly?
chapters.takeaway: Committee members challenged the lack of a major national awareness campaign, while the Minister argued that public warnings must offer useful advice and stopped short of promising one.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If air pollution is such a serious public health threat, shouldn't the Government run a national campaign explaining the risks and what people can do to reduce their exposure?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: We need to give people information they can actually use. The daily air quality index has been updated, people can sign up for local pollution alerts, and weather apps increasingly show air quality. DEFRA also brings together researchers, healthcare professionals and charities through the Air Pollution Awareness Coalition to improve communication. We keep reviewing whether more is needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you feel limited in what you can tell people because it might raise uncomfortable questions for other departments? Someone living beside a busy road may have no realistic way to escape the pollution. Are you reluctant to highlight a problem the Government can't easily solve?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: No, I don't feel that at all. The issue is making sure advice is useful. Trusted healthcare professionals can speak to people about their specific circumstances. We also have to reach vulnerable people who might not use phone apps or social media.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But the Government has run major campaigns about smoking, healthy eating, extreme heat and Covid. We're talking about roughly 30,000 deaths a year, and communities that face especially high risks may not even know it. Shouldn't we be doing more than relying on local doctors?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: I'm not ruling out a national campaign. We need to consider what information would help, how best to reach people and the cost. I can't announce a new campaign today. We'll consider the Committee's recommendations and the Chief Medical Officer's advice. We certainly need to do more to support healthcare professionals, and we'll keep the case for wider public communication under review.

chapters.title: Working together and learning from elsewhere
chapters.takeaway: Other countries offer practical examples of reducing pollution, but questions remain about whether all government departments and local decision-makers give public health enough attention.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: We've discussed cooperation between government departments. What about working with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and learning from other countries?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: I've only recently taken up this post, so I haven't yet met ministers from the other UK governments. Simon may be able to explain the existing arrangements.

turns.speaker: Simon Reeve
turns.text: Our department is responsible for health policy in England, but our scientific advisers work across the UK. That includes experts working through the UK Health Security Agency and a specialist committee studying the health effects of air pollution. We share scientific evidence across the different nations.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: England has the UK's biggest air pollution problem, particularly southern England. That's partly because of pollution arriving from Europe, but also because of population density and certain farming practices.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: The Netherlands and Canada have shown that farming emissions of ammonia can be cut substantially, by as much as half, through changes that can eventually pay for themselves. Making the initial changes is the difficult part. Other countries have also found effective ways to introduce electric vehicles rapidly in busy cities. We should learn from them.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: How seriously do departments responsible for government spending, business and overall policy take this? There are economic objections whenever cities introduce pollution controls. Manchester abandoned its proposed charging scheme and invested in cleaner buses instead. Decisions about vehicles and energy also affect health.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: All government departments have agreed to the ten-year health plan, which includes air pollution. I'll continue making the public health case as the air quality strategy is reviewed. Manchester illustrates why local decision-making matters. Its leaders chose investment in lower-emission and electric buses instead of a charging scheme. Different places may choose different methods, provided the aim is to reduce pollution.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Should planning authorities be legally required to consult local public health experts before approving developments? In my constituency, family homes have been built beside a bypass that will carry heavy traffic and lorries. Pollution wasn't properly discussed. With so many new homes planned nationally, shouldn't health have a bigger role in those decisions?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Local public health directors have an important part to play, and I want to support them. I'm happy to consider your suggestion about making consultation a requirement, but I can't say today whether that's the right approach.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: I'd strongly welcome more opportunities for public health experts to contribute to planning decisions. Their evidence would help local leaders understand the consequences of what they're approving. Whether consultation should be legally compulsory is a political decision, not one for me.

chapters.title: Stronger laws and the limits of progress
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses agreed that pollution must fall further, but left decisions about new legal rights and tighter limits to ministers while emphasising that past improvements show further progress is possible.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: What do you think of the proposed Clean Air (Human Rights) Bill, also called Ella's Law? It's named after Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, a nine-year-old girl who died in London in 2013. She was the first person in the UK to have air pollution formally recorded as a cause of death. The Bill would establish a right to clean air. Would that help achieve the improvements you've described?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Ella's tragic death, and her mother's tireless campaigning, have been enormously important in prompting action. I completely support the principle of learning from that experience and protecting others. But whether a particular law is the right way to achieve that is a decision for political leaders. I'm not going to take a position on the Bill itself.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Why hasn't the Government followed the EU in tightening pollution limits in response to WHO recommendations? Northern Ireland has been considering proposals to reduce its limits, including cutting the permitted concentration of PM2.5 from 25 to 10 micrograms per cubic metre. Why should people elsewhere in the UK have weaker protections?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: DEFRA is responsible for setting those limits, so its minister is best placed to answer. The forthcoming review of the air quality strategy will look at the evidence and provide an opportunity to consider these questions.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: From a medical perspective, we clearly need to go further in reducing pollution across several industries and activities. But deciding the precise legal limits is a matter for ministers. My role is to explain why further reductions would improve health.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Can you confirm how many deaths are currently attributed to air pollution?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: The central estimate is about 30,000 a year. It's calculated from research rather than obtained by counting individual deaths, but it's a reasonable estimate. And deaths are only part of the problem. Air pollution also causes illness and disability, from poor development before birth through to lung disease, heart disease, strokes and potentially dementia later in life.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Parliament spends considerable time discussing deaths from knife crime and road accidents, which are far fewer. Yet we're talking about around 30,000 deaths linked to air pollution. Haven't we failed to make progress?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: We have made progress, and that's important to recognise. A similar expert report about ten years ago estimated 40,000 deaths, compared with 30,000 now. Pollution has fallen in many areas, although not all. The improvement shows that action works.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: We can reduce pollution much further. The technical solutions exist, although putting them into practice won't be straightforward everywhere. Further reductions would prevent illness, help children develop healthier lungs and allow adults to live independently for longer. But improvements don't happen automatically. They happen because Parliament pushes for change, laws are updated and engineers develop better technology. We have to keep making that effort.
